To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified activating somatic mutations in the Smo gene in sporadic BCS, that these mutations can cooperate with adenomatous polyposis coli to transform rat fibroblast cells, and that overexpression of mutant SMO in transgenic mice results in the development of skin lesions similar to BCC.

we have found activating mutations in the gene encoding the transmembrane signalling protein Smoothened in human sporadic basal-cell carcinomas and have shown that these mutations are capable of cooperating with a viral oncogene to transform cultured cells and to induce skin abnormalities similar to those seen in basal-cell carcinomas in mice.
1) SMO is a component of the SHHH–receptor signalling complex; and 2) SMO mutations can activate the SHHH–SMO signalling cascade and cause basal cell carcinomas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and molecular basis of cancer.
the genetic basis of basal-cell carcinomas (BCs) and the molecular basis of the hedgehog signaling pathway.
the identification of the genetic alterations that underlie the formation of human cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SMO gene is a proto-oncogene and that its activation is involved in the genesis of BCCs.
SMO mutations are found only in BCCs and not in any other cancer.
the SHH–PTCH–SMO signalling pathway is involved in the genesis of BCCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway is a key regulator of embryonic development.
we have identified the first oncogenic mutation in a transmembrane protein in humans.
the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway plays an important role in the pathogenesis of basal cell carcinoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified mutations in SMO, which are oncogenic, in sporadic basal cell carcinoma.
SMO can function in human cancer, and that it can be targeted therapeutically.
we have identified the first somatic oncogenic mutations in SMO, a gene that is essential in the development of vertebrate embryos.
